memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: Abraham and Sarah were already very old, and Sarah was past the age of childbearing. So Sarah laughed to herself as she thought, "After I am worn out and my lord is old, will I now have this pleasure?" - Gen 18:11-12 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Sarah laughs - but hers is a different laugh from Abraham's. His was wonder tangled with worship; hers is quiet disbelief. "After I am worn out and my lord is old, will I now have this pleasure?" She has done the arithmetic of her body and her age, and it simply doesn't work. The promise seems not just delayed but biologically impossible.

We should be gentle with Sarah, because we understand her. She had waited decades. Hope deferred had made her heart weary. When you have wanted something for so long and it has never come, it can feel safer to laugh it off than to hope again and risk fresh disappointment. Sarah's laugh is the laugh of a worn-out heart protecting itself.

But notice what she said - "after I am worn out." She was measuring the promise by her own depleted resources. And that is exactly where so many of us stumble. We assess God's promises by what we can see in ourselves, and conclude they must be impossible.

Yet the whole point is that this was never about Sarah's ability. It was about God's power. Paul later celebrates that Abraham and Sarah's bodies were "as good as dead," and yet God gave life (Rom 4:19). When God's promise outstrips your resources entirely, that is not a reason to laugh it off - it is the very place God delights to display His power.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
- Do you measure God's promises by your own depleted resources?
- Has weariness made you laugh off hope instead of holding onto it?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Lord, forgive me for measuring Your promises by my own limits. When my resources are worn out, help me remember Your power is not. Renew my weary hope to trust in what only You can do.
Amen.
